# Rurumigarājajātaka (Ja 482)

**ID:** Ja 482
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Rurumigarājajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul12.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Rurumigarājajātaka* (Ja 482) is a Jātaka tale whose introductory narrative is set while the Buddha was dwelling at the Bamboo-grove (*Veḷuvana*). It was delivered regarding Devadatta, who claimed that the Buddha had done him no good whatever, maintaining that he had received ordination, learned the Three Baskets, and gained honor entirely through his own agency. In response to the monks discussing Devadatta's ingratitude in the Hall of Truth, the Buddha revealed that Devadatta had also shown gross ingratitude in a former existence after the Bodhisatta had saved his life. In Pali exegesis, the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* cites the Bodhisatta's birth as the Ruru deer king (*Rūrūmigarāja*) as an illustrative example of the supreme perfection of patience, specifically endurance-patience (*adhivāsanakkhanti*) [Endo 1997].

**Sources**

- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism: A Study of the Concept of Buddha in the Pali Commentaries (1997) — Noted the citation of Rūrūmigarāja in the Cariyāpiṭaka commentary to illustrate adhivāsanakkhanti.
